newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Foreign troops to make "D-Day" landing in Albania.
newsitem.headline: Foreign troops to make "D-Day" landing in Albania.

text.p: Albanians waited on Monday for the "D-Day" landing of nearly 1,200 Italian, French and Spanish troops as U.N. officials said the country's poor were desperately in need of food.

An eight-nation security force will begin deploying in earnest from Tuesday to protect the distribution of aid to the distressed Balkan state, which sank into anarchy after fraudulent savings schemes collapsed early this year.
The first major food aid shipment of more than 400 tonnes of wheat flour, beans and vegetable oil was expected in the main port of Durres at the same time the troops are due.
"D-day is tomorrow. It starts from after midnight," said Admiral Guido Venturoni, Italy's Defence Chief of Staff.
The operation is called "Dawn", symbolising a new beginning after an armed insurrection swept Europe's poorest nation. Nearly 300 have been killed in the mayhem.

Venturoni said in Rome that four navy vessels would dock on Tuesday in the main Albanian port of Durres with 450 French, 350 Spanish and 200 Italian soldiers after crossing the Adriatic from the Italian port of Brindisi.
A further 150 Italian paratroopers would land at Tirana airport on board six Italian military aircraft.
Venturoni said the force, expected to number 6,000 when fully deployed, would have up to 2,500 men in Albania within the first 10 days of its mission.
Greece, Turkey, Austria, Denmark and Romania are also contributing soldiers to the U.N.-backed mission.
Greek army chief Lieutenant-General Manoussos Paragioudakis said in Athens a company of Greek soldiers was expected in the southern rebel-held city of Vlore on Thursday on a ship from Salonika.
Another company was expected to land in Tirana on Saturday, flying in from Salonika.

Albania's poor desperately need food, the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said. Their basic food costs have shot up since the country slid into anarchy in February, their social security payments have stopped and state food supplies are not reaching orphanages or homes for the handicapped and elderly.

"There is no starvation in Albania, but there is a need for food assistance, especially for institutions such as orphanages and homes for the elderly and handicapped, and destitute families," WFP spokeswoman Laura Boldrini told Reuters.
"Furthermore, many families need assistance because they cannot afford to buy food which is more expensive."
The WFP will rely on the multinational mission to escort it in unsafe areas, Bordini said.
Some 150,000 families among Albania's 3.4 million people need food, according to the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs. Beggars are a common sight in Albania.
Amid signs that the government was making progress to restore order, the Albanian army staged a ceremony in Durres to show that it had regrouped a 400-strong infantry battalion.
The armed forces disintegrated as many soldiers deserted their posts during the uprising.
"The principal aim was to boost the morale of the soldiers," Defence Minister Shaqir Vukaj said. "We are working to reorganise the army in the whole of Albania."
Franz Vranitzky, European mediator of the Vienna-based Organisation for Security and Cooperation (OSCE), was due in Tirana to meet officials on Wednesday.

Albania's descent into chaos cast a shadow over bankers from East and West at the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) in London, showing how hard-won reforms can be wiped out almost overnight.
While free-market reforms seem irreversible in the more prosperous states of central Europe, Albania shows that change is tenuous in much of the rest of the post-communist world.
"Albania is a tragic illustration of how hard-won progress in transition can be lost with frightening speed," EBRD President Jacques de Larosiere said.
